subject: AI & Agents
title: Bias in Language Models
description: One-minute skill: Bias in Language Models.

hook.text: Ask an LLM to describe a CEO and it defaults to male. The bias came from training data.

buildup.text: LLMs absorb the biases present in the text they're trained on — societal, cultural, and historical.

discovery.text: Gender, racial, and cultural biases show up in word associations and default assumptions.

twist.text: Debiasing is hard. Remove one bias and you might amplify another or lose useful information.

climax.text: Researchers use RLHF and filtered data to reduce bias, but no model is truly neutral.

punchline.text: AI mirrors society's biases at scale.

quiz.question: Where do LLM biases come from?
options: From biases present in the training data
From the hardware they run on

details.summary: Language models inherit and sometimes amplify biases present in their training data: gender stereotypes, racial biases, cultural assumptions, and political leanings. These biases affect millions of users and decisions.
details.whyItMatters: Biased AI can perpetuate discrimination at scale. When language models inform hiring, lending, healthcare, and education decisions, even small biases cause real harm to real people.
takeaways: LLMs inherit biases from their training data
Biases include gender, racial, cultural, and political dimensions
Mitigating bias is an active area of research with no complete solution

faq.question: How do language models become biased?
faq.answer: Training data reflects historical and societal biases. If the internet contains more male CEO examples, the model associates leadership with men. These patterns are learned statistically and surface in outputs.

faq.question: Can bias in language models be eliminated?
faq.answer: Not completely with current techniques. RLHF, data filtering, and fine-tuning reduce measured biases but cannot eliminate all embedded associations. Ongoing monitoring and targeted corrections are the practical approach.
